[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#decision-summary]

## Decision Summary

Enterprise AI agent ecosystems built on citizen-development platforms require a governance model that allows domain teams to innovate locally while central architecture maintains policy consistency, quality standards, and lifecycle controls. This ADR establishes the federated governance model as the mandatory approach for all enterprise AI agent portfolios.

---
page_texts.5:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#context-and-problem-statement]

## Context and Problem Statement

- **Business Context**: Gainwell's adoption of M365 Copilot and AI agent platforms has reached a scale where multiple teams are building, publishing, and operating AI agents independently. Without a defined governance model, the portfolio is at risk of capability sprawl, inconsistent quality, unclear ownership, and uncontrolled compliance exposure.
- **Technical Context**: Citizen-development AI platforms (M365 Copilot Agent Builder, Copilot Studio) have a low barrier to entry, enabling rapid agent creation without requiring software engineering skills. This creates portfolio management challenges that do not exist in traditional software delivery.
- **Problem Statement**: The organization must choose a governance model that balances innovation speed with enterprise-level policy consistency, quality assurance, and lifecycle control across a growing and diverse AI agent portfolio.
page_texts.6:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#decision-drivers]

### Decision Drivers

- 📋 Enterprise compliance and policy consistency requirements across all AI agent outputs
- 🏗️ Citizen-development scale requires governance that does not require centralized review of every build
- ⚡ Domain teams need autonomy to evolve capabilities within their business context
- 🔍 Portfolio observability and lifecycle control are required to prevent sprawl and manage risk
- 📊 Quality standards must be enforceable without a central bottleneck for every agent promotion

---
page_texts.8:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#federated-governance-with-centralized-guardrails]

### Federated Governance with Centralized Guardrails

**Description**: A hub-and-spoke model in which a central architecture board and platform governance team define mandatory standards, policy baselines, and quality gates. Domain teams own capability definition, build, and evolution within those standards. The central hub operates the capability registry, approves new domains, and holds quality-gate sign-off authority for lifecycle promotion.

**Phase 1: Foundation**
Establish mandatory standards (agent definition, evidence access, output contracts, prompt governance, quality validation, telemetry, naming convention, system connections, change control, portfolio hygiene) and publish the capability registry. All existing agents are inventoried and brought into compliance or contained.

**Phase 2: Federated Delivery**
Domain teams build and operate agents within approved capability domains. High-Tech roles own quality-gate reviews; Mid-Tech and Low-Tech roles are primary agent authors within their domains. Governance cadences (monthly, quarterly, event-driven) are operational.

**Phase 3: Continuous Portfolio Optimization**
Telemetry feeds governance decisions. Portfolio rationalization is systematic. Citizen builder golden path is published and actively used. New capability domains require architecture board approval before work begins.

**Pros**:

- ✅ Scales citizen development without creating a central bottleneck for every build
- ✅ Policy consistency is maintained through shared guardrails, not per-agent review
- ✅ Domain teams retain ownership of business-context decisions
- ✅ Quality gates at lifecycle promotion points enforce standards without blocking all builds
- ✅ Portfolio observability and rationalization are built into the governance cadence

**Cons**:

- ❌ Requires upfront investment to define and publish mandatory standards before scaling
- ❌ Hub roles (architecture board, platform governance team) require dedicated capacity
- ❌ Compliance depends on domain teams following standards voluntarily between quality gates

---
page_texts.10:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#option-1-centralized-governance]

### Option 1: Centralized Governance

**Description**: All AI agent builds are reviewed, approved, and operated by a central team. No domain teams build independently.

**Pros**:

- ✅ Maximum consistency and policy control
- ✅ Single point of accountability for all agent quality

**Cons**:

- ❌ Central team becomes a bottleneck as portfolio scale increases
- ❌ Contradicts the self-service principle established in the SDLC AI Consumer Role Model
- ❌ Domain context knowledge is concentrated in the wrong team
- ❌ Does not scale to the citizen-development volume that M365 Copilot enables
page_texts.11:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#option-2-fully-decentralized-governance]

### Option 2: Fully Decentralized Governance

**Description**: Each domain team defines its own governance standards and operates independently with no central coordination.

**Pros**:

- ✅ Maximum autonomy for domain teams
- ✅ No central bottleneck for any build or change

**Cons**:

- ❌ No mechanism for cross-domain policy consistency
- ❌ Capability sprawl and duplicate solutions are uncontrolled
- ❌ Quality and compliance obligations cannot be audited at the enterprise level
- ❌ Ownership and support boundaries are unclear when assets are abandoned

[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#option-3-federated-governance-with-centralized-guardrails-selected]

### Option 3: Federated Governance with Centralized Guardrails (Selected)

See Required Option above.

page_texts.13:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#decision-outcome]

## Decision Outcome

**Chosen Option**: **Federated Governance with Centralized Guardrails**

**Rationale**: The federated model is the only option that scales to the citizen-development volume that M365 Copilot enables while maintaining enterprise-level policy consistency and lifecycle control. Centralized governance does not scale; fully decentralized governance does not provide the compliance and quality assurance required. The federated model is directly supported by the SDLC AI Consumer Role Model (High/Mid/Low-Tech tier definitions) which already establishes that High-Tech roles own standards and governance sign-off rather than individual agent builds.
page_texts.14:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#implementation]

### Implementation

- 🎯 **Key Steps**: Publish mandatory standards (STD-TEC-AI-001 through STD-TEC-AI-008, STD-GOV-AI-004, STD-GOV-AI-005); establish capability registry; define domain topology; activate governance cadences; publish citizen builder golden path
- 📊 **Success Criteria**: All Production agents have complete capability contracts and active owners; quality gate pass rate is measurable; portfolio rationalization reviews occur on the defined cadence; no unregistered Production capabilities

---
page_texts.16:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#-positive]

### ✅ Positive

- Domain teams can build and evolve agents without requiring central architecture review at every step
- Policy consistency is enforceable through shared guardrails and promotion-gate reviews
- Portfolio observability is built into governance structure, enabling data-driven rationalization
- The role model (High/Mid/Low-Tech) maps directly to the hub-and-spoke model without requiring new organizational constructs
page_texts.17:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#-negative]

### ❌ Negative

- Central hub roles (architecture board, platform governance team) require dedicated capacity that must be formally allocated
- Standards compliance between quality gates depends on domain team discipline, not hard platform enforcement
- Initial onboarding of existing agents to the registry and standards will require remediation effort
page_texts.18:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#-neutral]

### ⚪ Neutral

- Some platform governance controls must be implemented as process gates rather than automated platform enforcement, as documented in the M365 Copilot implementability validation
- Domain topology will require ongoing boundary review as the portfolio evolves

---
page_texts.20:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#-risks]

### ⚠️ Risks

- Domain teams may bypass quality gates under delivery pressure if the governance cadence is not actively managed
- Hub capacity constraints may create informal centralization as architects absorb review burden that should stay with domain owners
- Platform updates to M365 Copilot or Copilot Studio may change which governance controls can be enforced natively vs. by process
page_texts.21:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#-mitigations]

### 🛡️ Mitigations

- Monthly and quarterly governance cadences are mandatory, not advisory; domain owners report status to the architecture board
- High-Tech role responsibilities are explicitly bounded to quality-gate review and standards authorship, not individual agent builds, to prevent informal centralization
- Standards are written as platform-agnostic requirements with M365 Copilot implementation notes, allowing platform-specific enforcement guidance to be updated independently of the requirement

---
page_texts.22:
[decisions/governance/ADR-GOV-011-federated-ai-governance-model.md#compliance-notes]

## Compliance Notes

- **Security**: All AI agents operating on enterprise data must comply with data classification requirements and permission-trimmed access assumptions as defined in STD-TEC-AI-002. Agents handling regulated data (PII, compliance-relevant) require escalation per the role build capability alignment model.
- **Quality and Auditability**: AI outputs used in internal delivery workflows must meet provenance and auditability requirements as defined in STD-TEC-AI-003 and STD-TEC-AI-005, ensuring Gainwell's work products are traceable and defensible.
- **Standards**: This decision is the governance foundation for STD-TEC-AI-001 through STD-TEC-AI-008 and STD-GOV-AI-004 through STD-GOV-AI-005.
